doc.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015

title: Ruth on lonely weeks and the studio wives' clique
summary: Ruth recalls waiting at home with the children while Bucky worked all week, Saturday-night parties with the Corteses, and keeping the checkbook.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Okay. Well I really wanted to talk some more today about just following up — I know you did an awful lot of studio work. And Ruth you were talking about waiting for the husbands to get home?

It was lonely. I mean I had the children, thank goodness. But he was gone all week long and then maybe Saturday night we could get to go out if we had a sitter, babysitters. But I remember Dominick Cortese and his wife and somebody would have a party. It was like wow, we’re going out tonight. © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

That’s interesting that you say on Saturday night, because where I’m from, in Upstate New York, Saturday night is usually a night you’d be working. But during the studio years that might not have been — unless you had a jazz gig or something.

Well it wasn’t every Saturday night. But when the wives got together it was so much fun, and we could all give our point of view about this — I’d hate to say our husbands — but we’d always start to talk, “well what does he do,” — “well he does this, you know” and, “oh no, he never does that.” So we all had a little clique going there.
What kind of things would a wife say, “he never does that” meaning what?
It would be all different things. It’s not just music. It might be gardening or it might be —
Oh I see what you’re talking about.
Oh, he loves that” and I said, “oh I love that,” “oh my husband would never do that. You know, stuff like that.
Stuff like who’s at home, who balances the checkbook, who balances the checkbook in your family?

I did, up until recently. No but I did because we were just married and I think I had Ann already though, we lived in Clifton. And I always remember doing, he gave me, “here, you do it, the bank. Checking, cash and what was the other one, there was three of them, and we’d know exactly — savings, cash and checking. But anyway he’d give me the checks and whatever and I would sit at the kitchen table and do cash and this — and not even thinking of like gee we’d better put twenty dollars away or fifty dollars or a hundred. Don’t you think we ought to — no, we just automatically did savings, cash and I can’t think of what the other one was.
